title: Investors: Big super warns of tax change risk
full_text:
Aware Super head of infrastructure Mark Hector has warned broad tax changes risk turning foreign capital away from Australian shores, shrinking buyers for existing assets and infrastructure projects and hurting pension funds' returns.
As foreign institutional investors face higher capital gains taxes and restrictions on tax concessions, Hector said Australia's big super funds would suffer from the flight of foreign investors and there wouldn't be enough capital to fund the country's "AI hope".
"We consider it to be a net negative," Hector said of the changes at The Australian Financial Review Infrastructure Summit on Monday.
"Notwithstanding the massive size of the local pension fund system relative to our population, we have always been and always will be very reliant on foreign capital as well,
"So we do get concerned if we see the cumulative impacts of adverse tax changes leading to foreigners potentially deciding to reallocate their money elsewhere."
Hector's comments come after business groups earlier this year criticised broadening of the 30 per cent capital gains tax on foreign infrastructure investors. The changes include expanding the definition of taxable Australian real property, the principal asset test which pulled more sales into the Australian CGT net, and the requirement to formally notify transactions by foreign entities exceeding $20 million. The tax office has similarly targeted foreign investors restructuring into managed investment trusts which can receive a concessional 15 per cent tax treatment on infrastructure and real estate assets, while reserving the right to scrutinise transactions retrospectively for CGT obligations.
"I think in recent years there have been quite a few adverse changes. We've seen firsthand some of the implications that it has for their post tax returns, their implications for valuations," Hector said.
"So when the domestic funds want to recycle our capital, sell to other buyers, they form part of that buyer universe. So if it's impacting their valuations [and] it can indirectly impact us as well." As a $155 billion project pipeline in Australia threatens to stall, Hector said he wasn't convinced there was enough capital to fund all of the "AI hope".
The Australian Energy Market Operator estimates there to be 67GW of data centre projects in development. Equinix Australia managing director Jarrod Nink said "only a fraction" would be realised.
"We are reacting a little bit as an industry to a lot of potential projects that won't all reach fruition," Nink told the panel. "Certainly from an Equinix perspective, our approach is to announce very late once you're actually ready to go live, rather than too far ahead of the curve."
KKR director of Asia Pacific Infrastructure Lu Yan Li said Australia faced enormous scale and complexity in funding the national data centre build out, with a keen focus on project fundamentals.
"What I think will drive market share and drive the ability to succeed in this environment will be a combination of capital and balance sheet availability, the co-ordination expertise around bringing all the different elements together - whether it's permitting, power, grid, community consultations - and then lastly the execution discipline to really deliver true spec and on time for your customers because that is what they're ultimately looking for," Li said.
Despite the tax changes, Stonepeak head of Asia and the Middle East Hajir Naghdy said there were "tremendous opportunities" in Australia. "We talk about extraordinary demographic tailwinds in India, at 0.8 per cent, Philippines at a little over 1 per cent, Australia is right up there [at 1.5 per cent], obviously off a smaller base," Naghdy said.
"Data centres are an incredibly important area, but it is one of multiple sectors which need significant long-term planning, investment, and participation from the private sector."
He added Australia was playing an increasingly critical role in the expanding Asia region, with 60 per cent of cargo originating in the region staying in the region today.
"We see this regionalisation as growing, and we see the role of Australia only increasing in importance, and that's what makes it such a compelling destination for us," he said.
Nine Entertainment Co.
